title: Find Me the Worst Possible Place: Paul Farmer at Rwinkwavu
dek: In November 2004 Paul Farmer turned down a working hospital in Rwanda and asked for a harder place; Partners In Health rebuilt a ruin at Rwinkwavu.

story.event: Choosing the derelict Rwinkwavu site over a working hospital and reopening it as Partners In Health's first hospital in Rwanda
story.summary: In November 2004 Paul Farmer of Partners In Health turned down a functioning hospital site at Ruhengeri and asked Rwandan health officials for the worst place in the country; they took him to Rwinkwavu in eastern Rwanda, where derelict buildings once used by a Belgian mining company and as barracks during the 1994 genocide served a district of about 200,000 people with no doctor. With the Ministry of Health and the Clinton Foundation, PIH and its Rwandan sister organisation Inshuti Mu Buzima rebuilt the site and opened Rwinkwavu Hospital in the summer of 2005, adding a children's ward and an operating suite in 2006.
paragraphs: In November 2004 Paul Farmer was touring Rwanda with health officials, looking for a hospital site. He had agreed to bring the model Partners In Health had built over two decades in rural Haiti to a country still recovering from the 1994 genocide. The officials first showed him Ruhengeri, in the north-west, where a clean hospital already had staff and an X-ray machine. He turned it down. "Find me the worst possible place in the country," he later recalled saying.

He was not choosing blind. By his own account, four of Rwanda's 30 districts then had no district hospital, and PIH asked for places of greatest need, partly to show that good care was possible there. Around then a young man at a talk he gave at Princeton told him the model would never work in Rwanda, given its history of violence and division. Yet at village meetings in 2004 Farmer found people speaking openly about their HIV status. His explicit goal was to do in five years what had taken twenty in Haiti.

The officials took him to Rwinkwavu, two hours east of Kigali. Its hospital was a set of derelict buildings, used decades earlier by a Belgian mining company and then as military barracks during the genocide, the walls marked by bullet holes. "It was abandoned, dirty and scary," Farmer told The Boston Globe. The district's 200,000 people had no doctor; PIH's own report adds no electricity, few medicines and a handful of overworked nurses. With Rwanda's Ministry of Health and the Clinton Foundation, Farmer, Michael Rich and Rwandan and American colleagues rebuilt it, living in decaying mining-era housing, while Haitian colleagues came to live there and train staff. The hospital opened in the summer of 2005.

In February 2006 a 30-bed children's ward and malnutrition centre opened; that October an operating suite meant emergency obstetric cases no longer had to be sent to a hospital over an hour away. By early 2008 the hospital had 96 beds and saw about 250 patients a day, while PIH stayed barely three months ahead in funding. "I go to bed worrying about all the promises we've made," Farmer said. In 2012 he reflected that the best design came "when we could build from scratch and not have to redo."

quote.text: They assume the end and consider how and by what means it is to be attained; and if it seems to be produced by several means they consider by which it is most easily and best produced
quote.source_title: Nicomachean Ethics, tr. W. D. Ross, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
quote.connection: Aristotle expects someone sure of the end to look for the means by which it is reached most easily and best, as if that were one search. Farmer refused the easiest site on purpose, betting the hardest would prove more, and later said building from scratch worked better. The story leaves the two words apart.

reflection: Farmer's request sounds like bravado, but in his own telling it was also an argument: if the care worked where there was nothing, no one could say it only worked in easy places. He paid for that in rebuilt walls and in nights spent counting promises.

You will meet smaller versions of the choice: begin where the work is easiest to show, or where the need is sharpest. Neither is wrong. What helps is knowing which one you picked and why, and keeping your promises few enough to count, so the worry Farmer took to bed is something you carry rather than something that carries you.
invitation: Write down the promises you have made this week, at work and at home. Mark the one you can keep today, and leave the rest on the page until tomorrow.

cross_checks.claim: Farmer turned down a better-equipped site and asked to work where the need was greatest
The Rwinkwavu hospital was abandoned and derelict, with no doctor, when PIH arrived
The rebuilt hospital opened and was functioning during 2005
PIH worked with the Rwandan government and the Clinton Foundation
Rwinkwavu was where PIH began its work in Rwanda
A children's ward and an operating room were added in 2006

research_notes: Company field: written 'Inshuti Mu Buzima (PIH)', the Rwandan sister organisation's name with PIH's initials, because the repeat screen matched the word 'Health' in 'Partners In Health' against a different organisation (Indus Hospital & Health Network, Abdul Bari Khan, Korangi 2007); that is a shared word, not the same company. This is a different episode from the existing Cange edition (Haiti, 1983-1987): it is PIH's first site in Africa, chosen in November 2004 and opened in 2005. The founder field names Paul Farmer only: the slate paired him with Ophelia Dahl, but none of the sources for this episode describes a role for Dahl (PIH's executive director at the time) in choosing or rebuilding Rwinkwavu; her own published reports from the hospital date from 2011. Staffing disagrees: the Globe (2008) says there were 'no beds, no patients, no staff', PIH's January 2007 update says 'only a handful of overworked nurses', and early staff recalled in 2015 that there was no doctor and too few nurses; the story uses the no-doctor point that all agree on and PIH's handful of nurses, and does not say 'no staff'. Dates: the Globe dates the scouting trip to November 2004 and the opening to summer 2005; Farmer's 2012 lecture says the decision to bet on Rwanda was made in 2004 and that he attended village meetings in 2004, 'the year before we started'; PIH's 2007 update calls 2006 its second year in Rwanda. His Princeton talk is dated only 'maybe 2004' in the lecture, so the story says 'around that time'. Bed numbers grow over time: 96 beds in the Globe (April 2008); Bill Frist reported 110 beds in 2014; the story uses the 2008 figure with its date. The Globe's district population (200,000) is used; the lecture's figure of 400,000-500,000 without a hospital refers to Butaro, a later site, and is not used. The 'barely three months ahead in funding' point applies to PIH across its nine countries, per the Globe. The MIT lecture was given in May 2012; the quotations are from the official transcript PDF linked from the OCW page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/hst-s14-health-information-systems-to-improve-quality-of-care-in-resource-poor-settings-spring-2012/1uPv6pWVh68QBXK3cQ0C-lszadvX9E9Bj_transcript.pdf), which is generated from captions; one passage of Farmer's is mislabelled 'AUDIENCE' there. pih.org returns 403 to the verifier, so PIH pages are cited from Internet Archive copies. The Aristotle passage is about deliberation over means in general; it is applied here by analogy.
